transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-05 15:00 UTC
Duration: 57m
Attendees: Lena Martinez (Redwood AE), Tom Iqbal (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Aurelia ML), Mark Chen (Aurelia Infra), Evan Black (Aurelia CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
We talked through recent accuracy regressions seen by Aurelia after switching to INT8+GPTQ, possible root causes (layerwise entropy, cold KV-cache warmup), and deployment options for a VPC pilot. Redwood proposed a staged pilot: baseline FP16, then INT8 + selective FP8 for sensitive layers, with exercising warmup and KV-cache sticky options to reduce staleness. Action items and next steps agreed.

Topics: quantization tradeoffs (INT8 / FP8 / GPTQ / AWQ), KV cache warmup, batching effects on latency/throughput, VPC/on-prem pilot scope, security and KMS questions.

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena: Alright everyone thanks for joining on time. Quick quick intro, I'm Lena, AE at Redwood. Tom will drive the tech bits. Priya, do you want to kick off with what you saw last week?
[00:14] Priya: Yeah hi, thanks. So we switched some traffic to INT8 + GPTQ last Tuesday to reduce cost. Most requests are fine, but we started seeing a 1-3% drop in rouge-like metrics on our summarization jobs — it's subtle but consistent. Notably it shows up after longer context sessions and when KV cache hit rate is low.
[00:34] Tom: Okay that matches a pattern we've seen — when you quantize certain attention layers, you introduce small bias that amplifies over long recurrency with cold KV-cache. Also batching can mask or amplify the effect depending on alignment.
[00:50] Mark: To add, our staging latency improved by about 35% tokens/sec on INT8, but customer complaints pushed us to revert. We need to preserve the latency wins but not regress quality.
[01:05] Evan: We're not married to INT8, but cost is material. If there's a reliable hybrid that keeps accuracy we can buy in. Also need to make sure this works in our VPC — we can't send PII to hosted endpoints.
[01:20] Tom: Understood. High level: three knobs we usually play with — layerwise precision mixing (hot layers FP16/FP8), different quant algorithms (GPTQ vs AWQ vs post-training symmetric int8), and runtime fallbacks (on-err or per-route). Also warmup strategies for KV-cache to avoid cold-start drift.
[01:42] Priya: Can you expand on AWQ? We saw GPTQ mentioned in PRs but not AWQ.
[01:48] Tom: Sure, AWQ is an asymmetric weight quant method that often preserves more dynamic range in attention layers; in practice AWQ sometimes outperforms older GPTQ on certain LLMs for generation quality. But it's more sensitive to per-layer scale factors and sometimes incompatible with certain kernel fusions on older runtimes.
[02:12] Lena: Quick interjection — compatibility note: on Redwood Dedicated and Private we support both AWQ and GPTQ-flavored kernels, but kernel selection might change perf numbers by 5-10% depending on sequence length. We'll include that matrix in the doc.
[02:28] Mark: Kernel selection — is that automatic? We run on our own VPC so we want deterministic behavior for benchmarking.
[02:35] Tom: We can pin kernel variants in the model config. For the pilot we'll suggest pinning so you get consistent baselines. Automatic kernel selection is opt-in for production where we trade a bit of determinism for throughput wins.
[02:50] Priya: Back to the regression itself: the error seems correlated with long chat sessions and with prompt prefixes that include a lot of code snippets. Could that be tokenization interplay with quant errors?
[03:03] Tom: Absolutely possible. Code tokens have different embedding distributions and can exacerbate quant noise in feed-forward layers. Also if your prefix changes KV shapes frequently it can cause more cache churn — cold entries + quant noise = drift.
[03:20] Evan: You mentioned warmup strategies earlier. Can you outline a practical approach?
[03:25] Tom: Two pragmatic strategies: pre-warm with synthetic prompts that mimic session prefixes, or keep a sticky warm KV instance per user segment so their cache doesn't go cold between requests. There's also dynamic KV rehydration — if a cold-hit is detected we re-run a micro-batch in FP16 for the first N tokens to stabilize. That costs a little but recovers quality.
[03:50] Priya: Micro-batch FP16 for first N tokens — how much overhead?
[03:54] Tom: Usually 5-10% extra token compute for that session's first call. It's a tradeoff vs rollback to FP16 for whole request which is much more expensive.
[04:05] Mark: Is the micro-batch approach supported in Redwood's runtime today or is it custom?
[04:10] Tom: It's supported as a runtime policy in Private and Dedicated, we can enable a 'first-token-stabilize' flag in the model route. We'll show the config in the playbook.
[04:20] Priya: What about deterministic seeds and randomness — do GPTQ/AWQ introduce non-determinism? We saw small different outputs between runs with same seed.
[04:30] Tom: Good point — quantized kernels can expose pseudo-random rounding differences across kernels/platforms; stochastic rounding in AWQ variants can increase variance if not pinned. We recommend explicit RNG seeding and disabling stochastic rounding for critical evals. We'll include a checklist.
[04:49] Evan: Security and compliance — we need to validate KMS integration for private key storage. Also audit logs, SSO.
[04:57] Lena: We'll attach the security pack: SOC2, ISO, KMS integration guide for GCP/Azure/AWS HSM, SAML SSO notes, and audit log schema. For the pilot in your VPC, we can support customer-managed KMS and narrow network egress.
[05:12] Mark: Perfect. Another operational question: how do batching settings interact with latency SLOs? We run latency-sensitive UI calls and async background batching.
[05:22] Tom: Batching increases throughput but adds queuing latency. Redwood runtime supports per-route batching: you can set max_delay_ms and preferred_batch_size. For UI SLOs we'll suggest tiny max_delay (<=10ms) and small batch sizes; for background we can be aggressive. The playbook will show recommended knobs per workload.
[05:42] Priya: For the pilot, what's the proposed sequence?
[05:45] Lena: Staged: 1) Baseline FP16 perf/accuracy on your staging data. 2) INT8-only run to measure perf/cost/accuracy. 3) Hybrid: selective FP8/FP16 for sensitive layers (we'll propose candidates), AWQ/GPTQ variants tested. 4) Enable KV warmup sticky or first-token stabilize and test again. 5) Triage any deltas and propose fixes or fallbacks.
[06:10] Priya: How long does each stage take?
[06:12] Tom: With your existing test harness — around 2-3 days per stage to get stable metrics, so whole pilot ~10 days. We're proposing 1-week pilot but can extend if we hit regressions.
[06:23] Mark: Cost for pilot infra?
[06:25] Lena: We'll provide a cost estimate in the pricing snapshot; pilot cost is typically modest and we can offset with credits.
[06:30] Evan: If we find a systematic layerwise bias, what's the mitigation?
[06:35] Tom: Mitigations: mix precision (hot layers FP16/FP8), per-layer rescaling, small fine-tune or calibration of quant scales with representative calibration set, or fallback to FP16 for routes failing accuracy gates.
[06:50] Priya: Calibration — do you do full calibration or per-channel?
[06:53] Tom: We do per-channel scale calibration for weights, and activation ranges via KL or pctile heuristics. AWQ workflows often give better per-channel preservation for attention.
[07:05] Lena: Let's capture action items — Tom will spin up the pilot infra, Priya will share prompt suites, Lena will send security and playbook.
[07:12] Evan: Also want to invite your runtime engineer to the follow-up if we have regressions.
[07:16] Tom: Sure — I can be on the triage, and we'll add runtime lead if needed.
[07:20] Lena: Great — wrapping up. We'll share the perf spreadsheet and recommended layer list by Monday.
[07:26] Priya: Thanks everyone.
